title: 5 Myths About Holidaying With a Dog in Stari Grad
metaDescription: Dog beaches, ferries, restaurants, heat, vets and EU pet passport rules for Stari Grad on Hvar, with 2026 ferry prices and a clear dog-friendliness verdict.
content:
## Myth 1: "Stari Grad has a dog beach"

Stari Grad does not have a widely listed, officially designated *plaža za pse*. The town beaches, including Banj, are used by families and are not set up for dogs. Some sources describe parts of Banj as tolerating dogs. Treat that as unconfirmed and check signs on the day.

The nearest named dog beach on Hvar is Zaraće, a pebble bay on the south side of the island. It has a section reserved for dogs, is free to enter, and is about 6 km from Hvar Town. From Stari Grad, plan a drive across the island. Zaraće is also basic, so bring your own shade and water. Closer to Stari Grad, rocky platforms and pebble coves such as Žukova, a short walk from the parking area, suit dogs better than crowded town beaches.

**Better approach:** Use Stari Grad as a base and treat a dog beach as a day trip. Official dog beaches elsewhere in Dalmatia, such as Kašjuni in Split, are easy to combine with the ferry journey.

## Myth 2: "Dogs are only allowed on official dog beaches, and not in town"

Croatian dog rules are set by each town or municipality, so they vary. In general, a beach without a "no dogs" sign is usable, and an official dog beach simply adds amenities. Beach clubs, hotel beaches and the central swimming areas are the usual exceptions. Leash use is the default in public spaces. Carry a muzzle, because restricted breeds and some transport operators require one.

In the old town, dogs on a leash are normal on the waterfront and in the stone lanes. Restaurant terraces are the safe choice. Indoor dining is usually at the owner's discretion and often refused for hygiene reasons. Always ask before sitting down.

Hvar has no national park. The nearest are on other islands or on the mainland, such as Mljet and Krka. Dogs are usually restricted or leash-only there, so check each park's rules before planning a day trip. The UNESCO-listed Stari Grad Plain is open farmland. Leashed walking on the field paths is the best dog activity in the area.

**Insider perspective:** Most travelers overestimate the beach and underestimate the plain. Stari Grad's flat farm tracks and harbour promenade suit a dog on a long daily walk better than any single beach.

## Myth 3: "Ferries and catamarans are a hassle with a dog"

The route to Stari Grad is the easy one. Jadrolinija's car ferry (line 635) from Split takes about 2 hours. In the 2026 high season (29 May–27 Sep) an adult ticket costs €8.40 and a standard car €47.60, so a car plus driver is about €56 one way. Dogs travel free on Jadrolinija's larger ferries and stay on the open deck. Book the car space online in summer, because spaces on busy departures run out.

Catamarans are tighter. Jadrolinija's catamarans require a designated carrier on deck, a fee and a reservation. Krilo requires dogs to be muzzled and leashed. Catamarans also run to Hvar Town, not Stari Grad, and carry foot passengers only.

**Better approach:** Take the car ferry. Without a car, the Jadrolinija catamaran to Stari Grad costs about €10 per adult in summer, but confirm pet rules and book the carrier first.

## Myth 4: "Summer is the best time to bring a dog"

July and August bring afternoon temperatures above 30°C. Stone lanes, stairs and unshaded beaches are hard on paws and on breeds with short noses. Walk before 9:00 and after 19:00, and never leave a dog in a parked car.

The best months are May, June, September and October. The sea is warm enough to swim, the crowds are smaller, and a dog is easier to place at restaurants and accommodation. Ticks and sandflies are present in Dalmatia, so ask a vet about tick and leishmaniasis prevention before you go. Check your dog after each field walk.

**Accommodation:** Pet fees on Hvar usually run about €10–25 per night, and some hosts waive them or cap them per stay. Apartments with a ground-floor terrace or garden are easier than hotels. Confirm the fee and any size limit in writing before booking.

**Vet basics:** Croatia requires microchipping for all dogs. Stari Grad has limited veterinary services, and 24/7 emergency care is on the mainland, in Split. Save a Split clinic's number and ask your own vet for a pre-trip check.

## Myth 5: "Any pet passport covers Croatia"

The order matters. The dog needs an ISO microchip first, then a rabies vaccination, then at least 21 days of waiting before entry. A rabies shot dated before the chip is treated as invalid. The EU pet passport records all of this. A Croatian passport costs about €10.06 plus VAT at an authorised vet.

From 22 April 2026 the EU rules moved to Regulation 2026/131. For travellers little changed, and existing passports stay valid. From outside the EU, with a UK or US dog for example, an animal health certificate is used instead of the passport. Croatia does not require tapeworm treatment, but other countries on your route may.

## What to settle before booking Stari Grad with a dog

Check the vaccination dates first, then the ferry. Choose an apartment with outdoor space, and plan travel for late spring or early autumn. Book one dog beach day trip to Zaraće rather than expecting a beach in town.

**Verdict: Stari Grad is moderately dog-friendly, about 7 out of 10.** It is excellent for walking, calm to live in, and easy to reach by free dog ferry travel. It loses points for having no well-known official dog beach in town, limited indoor restaurant access and limited emergency vet care on the island. For a dog owner who wants quiet walks over a beach scene, it is one of the better bases on Hvar.

faq.question: Is there an official dog beach in Stari Grad?
faq.answer: There is no widely listed official plaža za pse in the town itself. The best-known designated dog beach on Hvar is Zaraće, on the south coast, with a section reserved for dogs and free entry. Closer to Stari Grad, rocky coves outside town are the practical choice, but check for signs.

faq.question: But isn't a dog allowed on every Croatian beach?
faq.answer: Not quite. Dogs are generally allowed where no sign forbids them, but town swimming areas, hotel beaches and beach clubs often restrict them. Rules are set by each municipality, so look for signage and use a leash.

faq.question: Do dogs pay on the ferry to Stari Grad?
faq.answer: Dogs travel free on Jadrolinija's larger car ferries and stay on the open deck. Catamarans are stricter: Jadrolinija requires a designated carrier with a fee and a reservation, and Krilo requires a muzzle and leash. Check current rules when booking.

faq.question: What documents does a dog need to enter Croatia from the EU?
faq.answer: An ISO microchip, a rabies vaccination given after the chip and at least 21 days before travel, and an EU pet passport issued by an authorised vet. Dogs from non-EU countries need an animal health certificate instead of the passport.

faq.question: When is the best time to visit Stari Grad with a dog?
faq.answer: May, June, September and October. Summer afternoons above 30°C make stone streets and open beaches uncomfortable for dogs, and peak-season crowds make restaurants and ferries harder to manage.

faq.question: What does accommodation charge for a dog?
faq.answer: Pet fees usually run about €10–25 per night, with some hosts waiving them or capping them per stay. Ask about the fee, size limits and whether the dog may be left alone before you book.

quickAnswer: The usual assumption is that a Croatian island town must have its own dog beach. Stari Grad does not have a well-known official plaža za pse. The real draw is flat harbour walks, quiet field paths, a free ferry for dogs, and rocky coves outside town. It works best in May, June, September and October.
